C:summary.t: Learn and practise forklift theory for your LF licence assessment — at your own pace, on any device.

C:description.t: Learn and practise the forklift theory you'll be assessed on for your LF High Risk Work Licence: WHS law and standards, hazards, ground conditions and weather, traffic management, pre-start and operational checks, faults and lock out/tag out, stability, rated capacity, load weight and load centre calculations, attachments, safe operating and stacking, shutdown, refuelling and recharging. Each module ends with a quiz, and a final practice exam helps you check your knowledge. An independent study aid to use alongside your training with an RTO — not nationally recognised training, and it does not give you a licence.

T:high-risk-work-licence.t: The forklift High Risk Work Licence

L:high-risk-work-licence:1.t: Operating a forklift is **high risk work** under Australia's Work Health and Safety (WHS) laws. To operate one you must hold a **High Risk Work Licence (HRWL)** for the right class — or be a trainee working under supervision while you train.

L:high-risk-work-licence:2.t:
| Class | Covers |
|---|---|
| **LF** | Forklift truck (counterbalance, reach trucks and similar) |
| **LO** | Order-picking forklift truck |

L:high-risk-work-licence:5.t: 2. Pass a knowledge **and** practical assessment with an **accredited assessor**.

L:high-risk-work-licence:6.t: 3. Apply to your state or territory regulator (e.g. SafeWork NSW, WorkSafe Victoria, WorkSafe Queensland) within the required time.

L:high-risk-work-licence:7.t: You must be **at least 18**. Licences are recognised nationally and must be renewed (generally every five years).

L:high-risk-work-licence:8.t: > This online course is theory preparation. It does not on its own give you a licence.

L:whs-duties:1.t: WHS laws (in Victoria, the OHS Act) place duties on everyone at a workplace.

L:whs-duties:2.t:
**The business (PCBU / employer) must**, so far as is reasonably practicable:
- provide safe plant — a forklift that is maintained and fit for use
- provide information, training, instruction and supervision
- set up safe systems of work, such as a **traffic management plan**

L:whs-duties:3.t:
**As an operator you must:**
- take reasonable care for your own health and safety
- take reasonable care that what you do (or don't do) doesn't harm others
- follow reasonable instructions, policies and **workplace procedures**
- **report hazards, incidents and defects**

L:whs-duties:5.t: Your instructions may come as a **verbal** instruction from a supervisor, a **written** job sheet, safe work procedure or SWMS, or an **electronic** work order on a scanner or tablet. Whatever form they take: read or listen carefully, ask questions if anything is unclear, and follow them.

T:standards-codes-records.t: Standards, codes of practice and records

L:standards-codes-records:1.t:
| Source | What it is |
|---|---|
| **WHS Act and Regulations** | The law. Must be followed. |
| **Codes of practice** | Practical guidance on meeting the law — e.g. Safe Work Australia's *Managing the risks of plant in the workplace*. Courts can use them as evidence of what is reasonably practicable. |
| **Australian Standards** | Technical requirements — e.g. the **AS 2359** series for powered industrial trucks (forklifts). |
| **Guidelines** | Further guidance — e.g. Safe Work Australia's *General guide for workplace traffic management*. |
| **Manufacturer's manual** | How *this* forklift must be operated, checked and maintained. |
| **Workplace procedures** | How *your site* does things — traffic plan, SWMS, emergency procedures. |

L:standards-codes-records:3.t: Good records prove checks were done and problems were followed up:

L:standards-codes-records:7.t: - **Maintenance and service records** for the forklift

L:standards-codes-records:8.t: - **Trainee logbook** — if you're training, record your supervised operating hours

L:standards-codes-records:9.t: Records must be **accurate, legible, dated and signed**, and kept where your workplace procedures say.

L:planning-and-communication:1.t: - **The load** — weight, size, shape, centre of gravity; is it stable and secure?

L:planning-and-communication:2.t: - **The forklift** — is the load within its **rated capacity**? Is the right attachment fitted?

L:planning-and-communication:3.t: - **The route** — surfaces, slopes, doorways, overhead clearances, blind corners.

L:planning-and-communication:4.t: - **The destination** — racking capacity, where the load will be placed.

L:planning-and-communication:5.t: - **People** — who else is working nearby, and how will you communicate?

L:planning-and-communication:7.t:
| Method | Use it for |
|---|---|
| **Warning devices** — horn, flashing beacon, reversing alarm, lights | Alerting people to the forklift |
| **Hand signals** | Directions from a spotter or observer. Agree the signals **before** starting. |
| **Two-way radio** | Coordinating over distance. Use clear, short messages and confirm you've understood. |
| **Signage and traffic warning systems** | Speed limits, pedestrian crossings, no-go zones, warning lights at doorways |
| **Written instructions** | Job sheets, work orders, SWMS, consignment paperwork |
| **Verbal instructions and questioning** | Ask questions to check you understand — e.g. "So you want these three pallets in bay 4, top level?" |

L:planning-and-communication:8.t: Always make **eye contact with pedestrians** before moving near them.

L:hazards-and-controls:1.t: - **Pedestrians**, other plant and vehicles — collision risk

L:hazards-and-controls:2.t: - **Overhead hazards** — powerlines (see the next lesson), low beams, doorways, sprinklers, lights, fixed structures

L:hazards-and-controls:4.t: - **Dangerous goods** — check labels/placards and the Safety Data Sheet (SDS); know the spill procedure

L:hazards-and-controls:5.t: - **Restricted or poorly ventilated areas** — LPG, petrol and diesel forklifts give off **carbon monoxide** in exhaust

L:hazards-and-controls:8.t: ## Hazard or risk — what's the difference?

L:hazards-and-controls:9.t: - A **hazard** is anything that **could cause harm** — injury, illness or damage. It's the *thing* or *situation*: a pedestrian near your work area, an oil spill, a powerline, a pothole, a damaged pallet.

L:hazards-and-controls:10.t: - A **risk** is the **chance that the hazard will actually hurt someone, and how bad it would be**. It's about *likelihood* and *consequence*.

L:hazards-and-controls:11.t:
| Hazard (what could cause harm) | Risk (how likely, and how bad) |
|---|---|
| Pedestrians walking through the loading area | Being struck by the forklift — likely in a busy area, and could be fatal |
| Oil spill on the floor | The forklift skids or someone slips — likely if it's on your route |
| Overhead powerline near the yard | Electrocution if the mast gets close — less likely if you plan, but the consequence is death |
| Damaged pallet | The load collapses or falls — injury or damaged stock |

L:hazards-and-controls:12.t: > **Spot the hazard → assess the risk → control it.** The hazard is the thing; the risk is how likely and how serious the harm is.

L:hazards-and-controls:14.t: Ask two questions about each hazard:

L:hazards-and-controls:15.t: 1. **Likelihood** — how likely is it to cause harm? (*Rare, possible, likely*)

L:hazards-and-controls:16.t: 2. **Consequence** — if it does, how bad would it be? (*Minor first aid, serious injury, death*)

L:hazards-and-controls:17.t: A hazard that is **likely** to happen **and** could cause **serious injury or death** is a **high risk** — fix it before you start work. Low risks still need controlling.

L:hazards-and-controls:19.t: 1. **Identify** the hazards — walk the route and look around before you start.

L:hazards-and-controls:21.t: 3. **Control** it using the hierarchy of control.

L:hazards-and-controls:22.t: 4. **Review** — are the controls working? Has anything changed?

L:hazards-and-controls:24.t: Use the most effective control you can, then work down:

L:hazards-and-controls:27.t: 3. **Isolate** people from it (barriers, separate walkways, exclusion zones)

L:hazards-and-controls:31.t: If a control is missing or not working, **report it**.

T:powerlines.t: Powerlines: keep clear, and the 5-step contact protocol

L:powerlines:1.t: Overhead powerlines are one of the deadliest hazards for forklift operators. Electricity can **jump (arc)** across a gap — you don't have to touch the line to be electrocuted. Treat **every line as live**.

L:powerlines:2.t: Before you start work outdoors or near doorways and awnings:

L:powerlines:3.t: - **Look up** — find every overhead line before you move or raise the mast.

L:powerlines:4.t: - **Keep the minimum approach distance** for your state and the line's voltage. For example, SafeWork NSW sets **3 m** for lines up to 132,000 volts, **6 m** up to 330,000 volts and **8 m** above that. Your site may set a bigger distance.

L:powerlines:5.t: - Remember lines **sag** in heat and **swing** in wind — and a raised mast or load is higher than you think.

L:powerlines:6.t: - **Lower the mast and tynes** before you travel near lines.

L:powerlines:7.t: - Use a **spotter** when working near lines, and ask for the power to be **switched off or the lines covered** if you have to work close to them.

L:powerlines:8.t: ## If the forklift touches a powerline — the 5 steps

L:powerlines:10.t: 1. **STAY on the forklift.** Stay calm, stay seated and don't touch any metal parts. The forklift may be live — the ground around it can be too.

L:powerlines:11.t: 2. **WARN others.** Shout to everyone to keep **at least 8 metres** away. No one should touch the forklift or try to help you.

L:powerlines:12.t: 3. **BREAK contact — only if it's safe.** Lower the mast or tynes, or drive the forklift clear of the line, but only if it won't cause another hazard.

L:powerlines:13.t: 4. **CALL for help.** Call **000** and the local electricity network operator (e.g. Ausgrid 13 13 88, Endeavour Energy 13 10 03, Essential Energy 13 20 80) and ask them to switch the power off. **Stay where you are** until they confirm the power is off.

L:powerlines:14.t: 5. **JUMP clear — only if you must** (e.g. the forklift is on fire). Jump well clear with your **feet together**, never touching the forklift and the ground at the same time. Land with feet together, then **shuffle or bunny-hop** with feet together until you are **at least 8 metres** away. **Never go back** until the power is confirmed off.

L:powerlines:16.t: - Don't use the forklift again until it has been **inspected**.

L:powerlines:17.t: - Report it to your supervisor straight away. Contact with a powerline is a **notifiable incident** — your employer must notify the WHS regulator.

L:powerlines:18.t: > If you see someone else's machine touching a line: **stay back at least 8 m**, call 000 and the network operator, and tell them to stay on the machine.

L:ground-and-weather:1.t: A loaded forklift is extremely heavy — the counterweight alone can weigh more than the load. Check the surface can take it.

L:ground-and-weather:2.t:
| Surface | Risk / what to do |
|---|---|
| **Backfilled ground** (e.g. over a trench) | May collapse — avoid unless confirmed compacted and suitable |
| **Soft soil, mud, sand** | Wheels sink, forklift can tip — avoid or use suitable equipment |
| **Hard compacted soil** | Usually OK, but check after rain |
| **Damaged or cracked concrete / bitumen, potholes** | Jolts the load and forklift — slow down, go around, report |
| **Railway tracks** | Cross slowly and at an angle where possible so wheels don't drop into the gap |
| **Rough or sloped terrain** | Instability — slow down, keep the load low, follow ramp rules |
| **Steel decks, grates, trench covers, dock plates** | Must be rated for the **combined weight** of forklift and load, and secured |

L:ground-and-weather:4.t:
| Condition | Response |
|---|---|
| **Strong wind** | Large flat loads (sheet material, boards) act like a sail — slow down or stop work if unsafe |
| **Lightning** | Stop outdoor work, park safely and take shelter |
| **Rain, wet or icy surfaces** | Reduce speed, brake and turn gently, allow much longer stopping distances |
| **Extreme heat** | Drink water, take breaks, watch for heat stress; watch engine temperature |
| **UV exposure** | Sun protection — hat, long sleeves, sunscreen, sunglasses |

L:ground-and-weather:5.t: If conditions make the job unsafe, **stop and tell your supervisor**.

T:traffic-management-exclusion-zones.t: Traffic management plans and exclusion zones

L:traffic-management-exclusion-zones:1.t: Workplaces where forklifts operate should have a **traffic management plan (TMP)**. It typically sets out:

L:traffic-management-exclusion-zones:2.t: - **forklift routes** and **pedestrian walkways**, separated where possible

L:traffic-management-exclusion-zones:6.t: - **signage**, line marking, mirrors and warning lights

L:traffic-management-exclusion-zones:7.t: - rules for visitors and delivery drivers

L:traffic-management-exclusion-zones:8.t: Know the TMP for your site and **follow it every time**.

L:traffic-management-exclusion-zones:10.t: An **exclusion zone** is an area around forklift work that people must not enter. Set one up with **barriers, bollards, cones, bunting and signs** — for example while loading a truck or stacking at height.

L:traffic-management-exclusion-zones:11.t: - Check the zone is in place before you start.

L:traffic-management-exclusion-zones:13.t: - If a control is missing or damaged (a broken barrier, a faded walkway, a mirror knocked out of position), **report it** to your supervisor.

L:pre-start-checks:1.t: Carry out a pre-start check **before every shift**, using the site checklist and the operator's manual. With the engine **off**, walk around and check:

L:pre-start-checks:2.t: - **Data plate** — present, legible, and **correct for the attachment fitted**

L:pre-start-checks:3.t: - **Structure** — look for **cracked or stressed welds** and **paint separation** (cracked or flaking paint at joints can show a crack underneath)

L:pre-start-checks:4.t: - **Tynes (forks) / attachments** — cracks, bends, heel wear; **locking pins in place** and attachments **secure**

L:pre-start-checks:5.t: - **Mast, chains and carriage** — damage, wear, chain tension

L:pre-start-checks:6.t: - **Hydraulics** — hoses, fittings and the ground underneath for **leaks**

L:pre-start-checks:7.t: - **Fluids** — engine oil, hydraulic oil, coolant, **fuel / LPG level**

L:pre-start-checks:8.t: - **Battery** (electric) — **charge level**, cables and connectors, no damage

L:pre-start-checks:9.t: - **Tyres and wheels** — damage, wear, **correct inflation**, wheel nuts

L:pre-start-checks:10.t: - **Overhead guard and load backrest** — fitted and undamaged

L:pre-start-checks:11.t: - **Lights, safety equipment** (e.g. fire extinguisher if fitted) and **signs and labels** — present and legible

L:pre-start-checks:12.t: - **Logbook / checklist** — available, and previous defects followed up

L:pre-start-checks:14.t: Use the steps and handholds and keep **three points of contact** (two hands and a foot, or two feet and a hand). Never jump down.

L:pre-start-checks:15.t: Once seated, **adjust the seat and mirrors** and **fasten and test the seatbelt**.

L:pre-start-checks:16.t: Record the check, and **record any damage** you find.

T:operational-checks-and-defects.t: Operational checks and lock out / tag out

L:operational-checks-and-defects:1.t: Start the forklift **as the manufacturer requires** and check:

L:operational-checks-and-defects:8.t: - **Hydraulics** — run lift, tilt and side shift through their **full range**; movement should be smooth

L:operational-checks-and-defects:11.t: Record the results on the checklist.

L:operational-checks-and-defects:13.t: If you find a fault, the forklift must not be used until it's fixed:

L:operational-checks-and-defects:15.t: 2. **Isolate** the power — turn off, remove the key, close the LPG valve or disconnect the battery as your procedure says.

L:operational-checks-and-defects:16.t: 3. **Tag** it — attach an "Out of service / Do not operate" tag (and a lock if your site uses them).

L:operational-checks-and-defects:17.t: 4. **Report** the fault to your supervisor and record it.

L:operational-checks-and-defects:18.t: Only an **authorised person** may remove the tag, once the repair is done and checked.

L:faults-failures-routine-problems:1.t:
| Failure | What to do |
|---|---|
| **Brake failure** | Take your foot off the accelerator, **warn others with the horn**, steer away from people and obstacles, and use the park brake to bring the forklift to a stop. Lower the load. Tag out and report. |
| **Steering failure** | Stop as quickly and safely as you can, warn others, lower the load. Tag out and report. |
| **Hydraulic failure** (load drops or won't hold) | Keep everyone clear of the load, stop, lower it if you can. Tag out and report. |
| **Forklift starts to tip** | **Do not jump.** Stay in the seat with the seatbelt on, hold the steering wheel firmly, brace your feet and **lean away** from the direction of the fall. |

L:faults-failures-routine-problems:2.t: Equipment failure on a ramp, at height or near people is very dangerous — which is why pre-start and operational checks matter.

L:faults-failures-routine-problems:4.t:
| Sign | Likely cause | Correction |
|---|---|---|
| Engine stutters / loses power (LPG) | Cylinder running empty | Park safely, change the cylinder following the procedure |
| Battery indicator low | Battery discharged | Return to the charging area; charge or swap |
| Hydraulics slow or jerky | Low hydraulic oil or a leak | Check the level per the manual; if leaking, **tag out** and report |
| Temperature gauge high | Overheating | Stop, shut down, let it cool — never open a hot radiator cap. Report it. |
| Light, horn or alarm not working | Globe, fuse or fault | Report it — don't operate until fixed |
| Tyre looks low or damaged | Puncture / wear | Report — repairs by a competent person only |

L:faults-failures-routine-problems:5.t: Only fix problems that are **within your competence** and allowed by your workplace procedures. Everything else: tag out and report.

T:stability-triangle.t: Centre of gravity and the stability triangle

L:stability-triangle:0.t: ## How a counterbalance forklift stays upright

L:stability-triangle:1.t: A counterbalance forklift works like a **see-saw**: the front wheels are the pivot (fulcrum), the load is on one side and the counterweight on the other.

L:stability-triangle:2.t: Most counterbalance forklifts have **three-point suspension**: the two front wheels and the pivot point of the rear axle. These form the **stability triangle**.

L:stability-triangle:3.t: - The **combined centre of gravity** of the forklift and load must stay **inside the stability triangle**.

L:stability-triangle:4.t: - If it moves outside, the forklift tips.

L:stability-triangle:6.t: - **Overloading** — lifting more than the rated capacity

L:stability-triangle:7.t: - **Lifting high** — raises the centre of gravity

L:stability-triangle:11.t: - **Ground giving way** — soft, backfilled or deteriorating ground

L:stability-triangle:13.t: - **Picking up or placing loads** carelessly — e.g. catching a rack, dropping a load

L:stability-triangle:14.t: - **Restricted spaces** that force tight turns or awkward approaches

L:stability-triangle:16.t: That's why you **travel with the load low and tilted back**, turn slowly, and never turn on a slope.

T:load-charts.t: The data plate and rated capacity

L:load-charts:1.t: Every forklift has a manufacturer's **data plate**. It shows the forklift's **rated capacity** — the **maximum weight it can safely lift**.

L:load-charts:2.t: > **Never lift more than the rated capacity.** If the load is heavier, don't lift it.

L:load-charts:3.t: The data plate also shows the **load centre** the capacity is rated at. The most common is **600 mm**.

L:load-charts:4.t: - **Load centre** — the distance from the vertical face of the tynes to the load's centre of gravity (the middle of its weight).

L:load-charts:5.t: - The rated capacity applies when the load centre is **no more than** the one on the data plate. If a load's centre of gravity is **further out** than that (for example a long crate), **don't lift it** — ask your supervisor.

L:load-charts:6.t: - **Attachments** — when an attachment is fitted, use the data plate for that attachment.

L:load-charts:8.t: Forklift A's data plate says **2,500 kg at a 600 mm load centre**. A pallet weighing **1,900 kg** with its load centre at **600 mm** is within capacity — **OK to lift**. A machine weighing **2,700 kg** is **200 kg over** — **don't lift it**.

L:load-charts:9.t: > Never add extra counterweight or put people on the back to "balance" a load.

L:load-charts:10.t: Only use attachments and modifications **approved by the manufacturer**, with a matching data plate.

T:working-out-load-weight.t: Working out the weight of a load

L:working-out-load-weight:0.t: ## Know the weight before you lift

L:working-out-load-weight:1.t: You can't check the load against the rated capacity if you don't know the weight. Ways to find it:

L:working-out-load-weight:2.t: - **Load labels and markings** on the item or pallet

L:working-out-load-weight:3.t: - **Consignment notes** and **running sheets** from the transport company

L:working-out-load-weight:5.t: - **Manufacturer's documentation** (e.g. for a machine or tank)

L:working-out-load-weight:6.t: - **The data plate** on equipment being moved (many machines show their own weight)

L:working-out-load-weight:7.t: - **Weighing** — weigh one carton and multiply, or use scales / a load-weighing indicator on the forklift

L:working-out-load-weight:8.t: If you can't confirm the weight — **don't lift it**. Ask your supervisor.

L:working-out-load-weight:10.t: **Total weight = (number of cartons × weight of one carton) + weight of the pallet**

L:working-out-load-weight:12.t: A pallet holds **5 layers of 8 cartons**. Each carton weighs **20 kg**. The pallet weighs **25 kg**.

L:working-out-load-weight:16.t: Then compare it with the forklift's **rated capacity** on the data plate. If 825 kg is less than or equal to the rated capacity, it's OK to lift.

L:working-out-load-weight:17.t: > **Count → Multiply → Add the pallet.** Use a calculator and write each step down — that's what you'll do in the assessment too.

L:attachments:1.t: An attachment **adds weight** to the front of the forklift and usually **moves the load centre forward**. Both reduce how much you can safely lift.

L:attachments:2.t: - Only fit attachments **approved by the manufacturer** for that forklift.

L:attachments:3.t: - The forklift must have a **data plate that covers the attachment**.

L:attachments:4.t: - Check the attachment is **secured** (locking pins, bolts, hydraulic connections) before use.

L:attachments:7.t:
| Attachment | Used for | Key safety points |
|---|---|---|
| **Side shifter** | Moving the tynes sideways to line up loads | Centre the load before travelling |
| **Fork extensions (slippers)** | Long or deep loads | Must be rated and the right size for the tynes, fully secured; capacity reduces |
| **Jib** | Lifting a load from a hook | The suspended load **swings** — move slowly; capacity varies by hook position |
| **Carpet spike / pole** | Carpet rolls, coils | Insert fully; watch for loads sliding off |
| **Drum carrier / clamp** | Drums | Drum must be gripped securely; liquids can slosh |
| **Bale clamp** | Bales (wool, cotton, hay, paper) | Correct clamp pressure — too little drops it, too much damages it |
| **Paper roll clamp** | Large paper rolls | Correct clamp pressure; rolls are heavy for their size |
| **Rotator** | Rotating or tipping loads | Rotating shifts the centre of gravity — rotate with the load low and the forklift stationary |
| **Personnel (work) platform** | Lifting people to work at height | Only a purpose-built platform designed for the forklift, secured to it, with the operator at the controls. **Never** lift people on the tynes or a pallet. |

L:unusual-loads:1.t: If the weight isn't centred, the centre of gravity shifts **sideways** and the forklift is easier to tip in a turn.

L:unusual-loads:2.t: - Position the tynes so the load is **centred** between them — use the side shift if fitted.

L:unusual-loads:3.t: - If a load is badly stacked, have it **restacked** before lifting.

L:unusual-loads:5.t: Long, wide, tall or odd-shaped loads (pipes, timber, machinery):

L:unusual-loads:6.t: - Spread the tynes **as wide as practical** for the load.

L:unusual-loads:7.t: - Allow **extra clearance** — long loads swing wide on turns.

L:unusual-loads:8.t: - Use an **observer** if the load blocks your view.

L:unusual-loads:11.t: A **dynamic load** moves while you're carrying it — liquids in drums or IBCs, or a load hanging from a jib. The movement adds force and shifts the centre of gravity.

L:unusual-loads:14.t: - Avoid sudden stops — a swinging load keeps moving.

L:unusual-loads:16.t: Use **gluts or dunnage** (timber blocks or bearers) under loads so the tynes can be inserted and withdrawn without damaging the load.

T:weights-and-quantities.t: Load weights: units, totals and maximum quantities

L:weights-and-quantities:1.t: Every load calculation uses the same few steps. Take it slowly, **use a calculator**, and **write each step down**.

L:weights-and-quantities:4.t: Rated capacity on the data plate is in **kilograms (kg)**. Paperwork sometimes uses **tonnes (t)**.

L:weights-and-quantities:5.t: **1 tonne = 1,000 kg.** To change tonnes into kilograms, **multiply by 1,000**.

L:weights-and-quantities:8.t: When a pallet has different items on it, **add every item, then add the pallet**.

L:weights-and-quantities:9.t:
> A pallet weighing **50 kg** carries items of **400 kg**, **350 kg** and **600 kg**.
> 400 + 350 + 600 = 1,350 kg → add the pallet: 1,350 + 50 = **1,400 kg**

L:weights-and-quantities:12.t: 2. **Multiply:** number of cartons × weight of one carton

L:weights-and-quantities:14.t:
> 5 layers of 10 cartons, 20 kg each, on a 30 kg pallet:
> 5 × 10 = 50 cartons → 50 × 20 = 1,000 kg → 1,000 + 30 = **1,030 kg**

L:weights-and-quantities:16.t: A weighbridge weighs the whole truck. **Load = loaded truck − empty truck.**

L:weights-and-quantities:17.t:
> Loaded truck **18,000 kg**, empty truck **12,000 kg** → load = **6,000 kg**.
> If that's **4 identical pallets**: 6,000 ÷ 4 = **1,500 kg each**.

L:weights-and-quantities:18.t: ## The most cartons you can carry

L:weights-and-quantities:19.t: 1. Take the pallet off the limit: **limit − pallet**

L:weights-and-quantities:20.t: 2. Divide by the weight of one carton

L:weights-and-quantities:21.t: 3. If the answer has a decimal, **round DOWN** — never up

L:weights-and-quantities:22.t:
> Limit **1,000 kg**, pallet **20 kg**, cartons **30 kg** each:
> 1,000 − 20 = 980 → 980 ÷ 30 = 32.67 → **32 cartons**.
> Check: 33 cartons would be 33 × 30 + 20 = **1,010 kg** — over the limit.

L:working-out-load-centre:1.t: The **load centre** is the distance from the **front face of the tynes** (where the load sits against the backrest) to the **middle of the load's weight** (its centre of gravity).

L:working-out-load-centre:2.t: Most forklift data plates are rated at a **600 mm** load centre.

L:working-out-load-centre:3.t: ## Even loads pushed hard against the backrest

L:working-out-load-centre:4.t: If the weight is spread evenly, the centre of gravity is in the **middle** of the load.

L:working-out-load-centre:5.t: **Load centre = depth of the load ÷ 2** (half the depth)

L:working-out-load-centre:6.t: > A crate **1,200 mm** deep, pushed hard against the backrest → 1,200 ÷ 2 = **600 mm**.

L:working-out-load-centre:8.t: If the load **isn't hard against the backrest**, add the gap.

L:working-out-load-centre:10.t: > A **1,000 mm** deep load sitting **200 mm** away from the backrest → 200 + 500 = **700 mm**.

L:working-out-load-centre:11.t: That's why you **insert the tynes fully** — a gap pushes the load centre forward, past the 600 mm the rated capacity is based on. If the load centre is more than the data plate's load centre, **don't lift** — ask your supervisor.

L:working-out-load-centre:13.t: If one end is heavier (e.g. a machine with the motor at one end), the centre of gravity **isn't in the middle**. Check markings or paperwork for the centre of gravity, put the **heavy end towards the mast**, and ask your supervisor if you're unsure.

T:reading-a-load-chart.t: Checking a load against rated capacity, step by step

L:reading-a-load-chart:1.t: 1. **Weight** — work out how heavy the load is (Count → Multiply → Add the pallet).

L:reading-a-load-chart:2.t: 2. **Load centre** — check the load's centre is **no more than** the data plate's load centre (usually **600 mm**). If it's further out, **don't lift** — ask your supervisor.

L:reading-a-load-chart:3.t: 3. **Compare** — is the load **less than or equal to** the **rated capacity**? Yes → OK to lift. No → **do not lift**.

L:reading-a-load-chart:5.t: **Forklift A — rated capacity 2,500 kg at a 600 mm load centre.**

L:reading-a-load-chart:7.t:
A pallet weighs **1,900 kg** and its load centre is **600 mm**.
1,900 is less than 2,500 → **OK to lift.** You have 2,500 − 1,900 = **600 kg** to spare.

L:reading-a-load-chart:9.t:
A crate weighs **2.7 t**. 2.7 × 1,000 = **2,700 kg**.
2,700 is more than 2,500 → **Do not lift** — it's **200 kg over**.

L:reading-a-load-chart:11.t:
48 cartons of **50 kg** on a **30 kg** pallet: 48 × 50 = 2,400 → + 30 = **2,430 kg**.
2,430 is less than 2,500 → **OK to lift**, with **70 kg** to spare.

L:reading-a-load-chart:12.t: ## Worked example 4 — the most you can lift

L:reading-a-load-chart:13.t:
How many **600 kg** drums can Forklift A carry at once (on a drum carrier rated 2,500 kg)?
2,500 ÷ 600 = 4.17 → round **down** → **4 drums** (2,400 kg). Five would be 3,000 kg — too heavy.

L:reading-a-load-chart:14.t: > If the answer has a decimal, **always round down**. Rounding up puts you over the rated capacity.

L:travelling-safely:2.t: - Travel with the load **low** — just high enough to clear the ground and suit the surface (commonly around 100–150 mm) — and the mast **tilted back**.

L:travelling-safely:3.t: - Keep a **safe speed** for the load, surface and surroundings, within site limits.

L:travelling-safely:4.t: - **Look in the direction of travel.** If the load blocks your forward view, **travel in reverse** or use an **observer (spotter)**.

L:travelling-safely:5.t: - Use your **mirrors** and **sound the horn** at blind corners, doorways and intersections.

L:travelling-safely:6.t: - Turn **slowly** — especially when carrying a load.

L:travelling-safely:8.t: - Keep arms, legs and head **inside** the overhead guard.

L:travelling-safely:10.t: - **Loaded:** keep the **load on the uphill side** — drive **forwards up**, **reverse down**.

L:travelling-safely:11.t: - **Unloaded:** keep the **tynes pointing downhill** — reverse up, drive forwards down.

L:travelling-safely:12.t: - **Never turn** on a ramp or slope, and never travel across it.

L:travelling-safely:14.t: Follow the traffic management plan, use forklift routes, make eye contact, and **stop** if anyone enters your work area.

T:picking-up-and-stacking.t: Picking up, the trial lift and stacking

L:picking-up-and-stacking:1.t: 1. Approach **slowly and squarely**, tynes level, at the right height.

L:picking-up-and-stacking:2.t: 2. **Position the tynes** to suit the pallet or load — spread as wide as practical, load centred.

L:picking-up-and-stacking:3.t: 3. Insert the tynes **fully**, so the load is against the backrest.

L:picking-up-and-stacking:4.t: 4. **Trial lift:** lift the load just clear of its support and check — is the forklift stable? Is the load secure and balanced? If the rear wheels feel light or anything moves, **lower it straight away** and reassess.

L:picking-up-and-stacking:5.t: 5. **Tilt back** slightly, check behind you, and reverse out slowly.

L:picking-up-and-stacking:6.t: 6. **Lower to travel height** before moving off.

L:picking-up-and-stacking:8.t: - Check the **racking is compliant** and its capacity suits the load.

L:picking-up-and-stacking:9.t: - Approach squarely and **stop** before the rack.

L:picking-up-and-stacking:10.t: - Only raise or lower the load **when stationary**.

L:picking-up-and-stacking:11.t: - Raise to the required height, **level the tynes**, then **inch forward**.

L:picking-up-and-stacking:12.t: - Use **tilt and side shift** to position the load accurately.

L:picking-up-and-stacking:13.t: - Lower onto the beams, withdraw the tynes, then lower to travel height before moving.

L:picking-up-and-stacking:14.t: Use an **observer** whenever your view is restricted — agree hand signals first.

L:picking-up-and-stacking:15.t: ## Placing on an elevated flat surface (e.g. a mezzanine or truck deck)

L:picking-up-and-stacking:16.t: The surface must be **flat, stable and strong enough**. Use **gluts or dunnage** under unpalletised loads so you can withdraw the tynes cleanly.

L:loading-trucks:1.t: - Check the truck **can't move** — handbrake on, wheels chocked or vehicle restraint engaged, driver in a safe area away from the loading zone.

L:loading-trucks:2.t: - Set up an **exclusion zone** around the truck.

L:loading-trucks:3.t: - Check **dock plates** are secure and rated for the forklift plus load.

L:loading-trucks:4.t: - Check the trailer floor is sound and can take the weight.

L:loading-trucks:5.t: - Watch for **dock edges** — keep well back.

L:loading-trucks:8.t: - Make sure the ground is **firm and level**.

L:loading-trucks:9.t: - Watch for loads shifting on the deck when straps are removed — **check before unstrapping**.

L:shutting-down:1.t: Park in a **designated safe area** — never on a slope, and never blocking exits, walkways, fire equipment or electrical switchboards.

L:shutting-down:4.t: 3. **Lower the tynes** (or attachment) fully to the ground, tilted forward so the tips rest on the floor.

L:shutting-down:5.t: 4. Shut down as the manufacturer requires, **isolate the power source** (e.g. LPG valve or battery isolator, per site procedure) and **remove the key**.

L:shutting-down:7.t: 6. Do a **post-operational check** and record and report any defects from the shift.

L:lpg-and-batteries:1.t: - Only in a **well-ventilated area**, away from ignition sources — **no smoking** or naked flames.

L:lpg-and-batteries:2.t: - Wear **PPE** — gloves and eye protection. LPG can cause **cold burns**.

L:lpg-and-batteries:3.t: - **Close the cylinder valve** and let the engine run until it stops, then turn the ignition off.

L:lpg-and-batteries:4.t: - Disconnect and remove the cylinder; check the new cylinder's **valve, O-ring/seal and connection** for damage.

L:lpg-and-batteries:5.t: - Fit it with the **locating pin** in place and the cylinder secured.

L:lpg-and-batteries:6.t: - Open the valve slowly and **check for leaks** with soapy water or leak-detection solution — **never a flame**.

L:lpg-and-batteries:8.t: - Engine **off**, no smoking, in the designated refuelling area.

L:lpg-and-batteries:9.t: - Don't overfill; clean up spills straight away.

L:lpg-and-batteries:12.t: - Charging gives off **hydrogen gas**, which is explosive — the area must be **ventilated** and free of ignition sources.

L:lpg-and-batteries:13.t: - Wear **PPE** — battery acid is corrosive. Know where the **eyewash** station is.

L:lpg-and-batteries:14.t: - **Turn the charger off before connecting or disconnecting** the battery, to avoid sparks.

L:lpg-and-batteries:15.t: - Check cables and plugs for damage; follow the manufacturer's instructions for electrolyte levels.

V:1:0:0.t: Welcome to Module 1. In this short video we'll cover why you need a licence to drive a forklift, your duties under safety law, and where the safety rules come from.

V:1:1:0.t: Forklifts work in busy places like this, close to people, racking and other vehicles.

V:1:1:1.t: One mistake can injure or kill someone. That's why the law treats forklift driving as high risk work.

V:1:2:0.t: Driving a forklift is high risk work. To do it, you need a High Risk Work Licence, class L F.

V:1:2:1.t: There's also a class L O, for order-picking forklifts. This course prepares you for class L F.

V:1:3:0.t: Here's how you get your licence.

V:1:3:1.t: First, train with a Registered Training Organisation.

V:1:3:2.t: Second, pass both a theory and a practical assessment with an accredited assessor.

V:1:3:3.t: Third, apply to your state or territory regulator. You must be at least eighteen, and you'll renew the licence about every five years.

V:1:4:0.t: Everyone at work has safety duties. The business must do three main things.

V:1:4:1.t: Provide a forklift that's safe and properly maintained.

V:1:4:2.t: Give you the training, information and supervision you need.

V:1:4:3.t: And set up safe ways of working, like a traffic management plan.

V:1:5:0.t: As the operator, you have duties too.

V:1:5:1.t: Take care of your own safety.

V:1:5:2.t: Take care that what you do doesn't hurt anyone else.

V:1:5:3.t: Follow reasonable instructions and your site's procedures. If you don't understand an instruction, ask.

V:1:5:4.t: And report every hazard, incident and defect you find.

V:1:6:0.t: Safety rules come from a few places.

V:1:6:1.t: The Work Health and Safety Act and Regulations. That's the law.

V:1:6:2.t: Codes of practice, which explain how to meet the law.

V:1:6:3.t: Australian Standards. For forklifts, that's the A S twenty-three fifty-nine series.

V:1:6:4.t: The manufacturer's manual for the forklift you're driving.

V:1:7:0.t: Good records show checks were done and problems were fixed. Make them accurate, neat, dated and signed.

V:1:7:1.t: Fill in a pre-start checklist every shift.

V:1:7:2.t: Write up defect and fault reports.

V:1:7:3.t: Report incidents, and near misses too.

V:1:7:4.t: And if you're a trainee, keep your logbook of supervised hours up to date.

V:1:8:0.t: That's Module 1. Next, read through the lessons, then take the quiz. And remember: if you're not sure, stop and ask.

V:2:0:0.t: Module 2 is about planning your work and spotting hazards before they hurt someone — including what to do if you hit a powerline.

V:2:1:0.t: Before you lift anything, think the job through.

V:2:1:1.t: The load. How heavy is it, how big, and is it secure?

V:2:1:2.t: The forklift. Can it lift this load, as high as you need?

V:2:1:3.t: The route. Check the ground, slopes, doorways and anything overhead.

V:2:1:4.t: The destination. Where exactly will the load go?

V:2:1:5.t: And people. Who else is working nearby, and how will you talk to them?

V:2:2:1.t: Use your horn, beacon and reversing alarm.

V:2:2:2.t: If a spotter is guiding you with hand signals, agree on the signals before you start.

V:2:2:3.t: On a two-way radio, keep messages short and clear, and confirm you understood.

V:2:2:4.t: And always make eye contact with pedestrians before you move near them.

V:2:3:0.t: Two words you need to know: hazard and risk. They're not the same thing.

V:2:3:1.t: A hazard is anything that could cause harm. A pedestrian near your work, an oil spill, a powerline, a damaged pallet.

V:2:3:2.t: A risk is the chance that the hazard will actually hurt someone.

V:2:3:3.t: And how bad the harm would be. A hazard that's likely to happen, and could kill someone, is a high risk.

V:2:3:4.t: So: spot the hazard, assess the risk by asking how likely and how bad, then control it.

V:2:4:0.t: When you find a hazard, use the hierarchy of control. Start at the top — the most effective — and work down.

V:2:4:2.t: Two. Substitute it with something safer.

V:2:4:3.t: Three. Isolate people from it, with barriers or separate walkways.

V:2:4:4.t: Four. Engineering controls, like mirrors and warning lights.

V:2:4:5.t: Five. Administrative controls, like procedures, signs and training.

V:2:4:6.t: Six. Personal protective equipment. That's the last line of defence.

V:2:5:0.t: When you work outside, always look up before you lift.

V:2:5:1.t: High-voltage electricity can jump across a gap, so you don't have to touch a powerline to be killed by it.

V:2:6:0.t: Overhead powerlines can kill. Electricity can jump across a gap, so you don't even have to touch the line.

V:2:6:1.t: Always look up. Keep the minimum distance for your state. In New South Wales, that's three metres for most local lines, and more for bigger lines.

V:2:6:2.t: Lower the mast before you travel, and use a spotter when you're working near lines.

V:2:7:0.t: If your forklift touches a powerline, remember five steps. Stay. Warn. Break. Call. Jump.

V:2:7:1.t: Step one. Stay on the forklift. Stay calm, and don't touch any metal parts.

V:2:7:2.t: Step two. Warn everyone to keep at least eight metres away. Nobody touches the forklift.

V:2:7:3.t: Step three. Break contact, by lowering the mast or driving clear — but only if it's safe.

V:2:7:4.t: Step four. Call triple zero and the electricity company, and ask them to turn the power off. Stay where you are until they say it's off.

V:2:7:5.t: Step five. Only if you must get off — for example, if there's a fire — jump clear.

V:2:8:0.t: The ground around a live forklift can be live too. That's why the eight metre rule matters.

V:2:8:1.t: Everyone else stays at least eight metres away, and no one tries to help you until the power is confirmed off.

V:2:9:0.t: If you have to get off, jump well clear with your feet together. Never touch the forklift and the ground at the same time.

V:2:9:1.t: Land with your feet together. Then shuffle or bunny-hop, keeping your feet together, until you're at least eight metres away.

V:2:9:2.t: Don't go back until the electricity company confirms the power is off. Then report it — it's a notifiable incident.

V:2:10:0.t: A loaded forklift is very heavy. Check the ground can take it.

V:2:10:1.t: Potholes and cracked concrete jolt the load. Slow down, or go around them, and report them.

V:2:10:2.t: Soft soil and backfilled trenches can collapse. Avoid them.

V:2:10:3.t: Cross railway tracks slowly, at an angle if you can.

V:2:10:4.t: And steel plates, grates and trench covers must be rated for the forklift and the load together.

V:2:11:1.t: In strong wind, big flat loads like sheets of plywood catch the wind like a sail.

V:2:11:2.t: If there's lightning, stop work, park safely, and take shelter.

V:2:11:3.t: On wet or icy ground, slow down, brake gently, and leave a much bigger stopping distance.

V:2:11:4.t: In heat, drink water, take breaks, and protect yourself from the sun.

V:2:12:0.t: In a real warehouse, people walk the same aisles you drive.

V:2:12:1.t: Marked walkways, barriers and exclusion zones keep pedestrians and forklifts apart.

V:2:13:0.t: A traffic management plan keeps people and forklifts apart, with walkways, crossings, speed limits and signs. Follow it every time.

V:2:13:1.t: When you're loading a truck or stacking high, set up an exclusion zone with barriers and signs.

V:2:13:2.t: If anyone walks into it, stop work until they've left.

V:2:14:0.t: That's Module 2. Remember the powerline steps: stay, warn, break, call, jump. Now read the lessons and try the quiz.

V:3:0:0.t: Module 3 covers the checks you do every shift, what to do when you find a fault, and what to do if something fails while you're driving.

V:3:1:0.t: Before every shift, you check the forklift, inside and out.

V:3:1:1.t: That includes the seat, seatbelt, controls and gauges, as well as the outside of the machine.

V:3:2:0.t: Do a pre-start check before every shift, with the engine off. Walk all the way around the forklift.

V:3:2:1.t: One. The tynes. Look for cracks, bends and wear, and check the locking pins.

V:3:2:2.t: Two. The mast and chains. Look for damage and worn or loose chains.

V:3:2:3.t: Three. Hydraulic hoses. Check for leaks, and look at the ground underneath.

V:3:2:4.t: Four. Tyres and wheels. Check for damage, wear and the right pressure.

V:3:2:5.t: Five. The overhead guard and load backrest must be fitted and undamaged.

V:3:2:6.t: Six. The data plate must be there, readable, and match any attachment.

V:3:2:7.t: Seven. Fluids and fuel — oil, coolant, and the gas bottle or battery charge.

V:3:3:0.t: Getting on and off is where a lot of injuries happen.

V:3:3:1.t: Use the steps and handholds with three points of contact. Never jump down.

V:3:3:2.t: Once you're seated, adjust the seat and mirrors.

V:3:3:3.t: Put your seatbelt on, and check it works.

V:3:4:0.t: Next, start the forklift the way the manufacturer says, and do your operational checks.

V:3:4:1.t: Test the horn, lights, beacon and reversing alarm.

V:3:4:3.t: Run the lift, tilt and side shift through their full range. They should move smoothly.

V:3:4:4.t: Check the brakes, steering and transmission.

V:3:4:5.t: And listen for any unusual noises. Write the results on your checklist.

V:3:5:0.t: If you find a fault, the forklift can't be used until it's fixed. This is called lock out, tag out.

V:3:5:2.t: Isolate the power. Take the key out, turn the gas off, or disconnect the battery.

V:3:5:4.t: Report the fault to your supervisor, and write it down.

V:3:6:0.t: The tag tells everyone the forklift must not be used. Only an authorised person can take it off, once the repair has been done and checked.

V:3:7:0.t: Sometimes things fail while you're driving.

V:3:7:1.t: If the brakes fail, take your foot off the accelerator, use the horn to warn people, steer away from people and obstacles, and use the park brake to stop.

V:3:7:2.t: If the steering fails, stop as safely as you can and warn people.

V:3:7:3.t: If the hydraulics fail and the load drops, keep everyone clear of it. In every case, tag out and report.

V:3:8:0.t: If the forklift starts to tip over, do not jump. People who jump are often crushed by the overhead guard.

V:3:8:1.t: Stay in the seat with your seatbelt on. Hold the steering wheel tight, brace your feet, and lean away from the direction it's falling.

V:3:9:1.t: If a gas forklift starts to stutter, the bottle is probably running empty. Park safely and change it.

V:3:9:2.t: If the battery is low, go back to the charging area.

V:3:9:3.t: If it's overheating, stop, turn it off and let it cool. Never open a hot radiator cap.

V:3:9:4.t: If a light, horn or alarm isn't working, report it. Only fix things you're trained and allowed to fix.

V:3:10:0.t: That's Module 3. Check it every shift, tag it if it's faulty, and report it. Now read the lessons and try the quiz.

V:4:0:0.t: Module 4 explains why forklifts tip over, how to read the data plate, how to work out a load's weight, and how attachments change things.

V:4:1:0.t: A counterbalance forklift works like a see-saw. The front wheels are the pivot. The load is on one side, and the heavy counterweight is on the other.

V:4:1:1.t: Seen from above, the two front wheels and the middle of the back axle make a triangle. This is the stability triangle.

V:4:1:2.t: The centre of gravity of the forklift and load together must stay inside this triangle.

V:4:2:0.t: If the centre of gravity moves outside the triangle, the forklift tips over.

V:4:2:1.t: It moves when you overload, lift high, tilt forward with a raised load, turn too fast, brake hard, or drive on a slope. That's why you travel with the load low and tilted back.

V:4:3:0.t: Every forklift has a data plate. It shows the rated capacity: the most weight the forklift can safely lift.

V:4:3:1.t: It also shows the load centre the capacity is rated at, usually six hundred millimetres. That's the distance from the front of the tynes to the middle of the load.

V:4:3:2.t: Never lift more than the rated capacity. And if the load's centre is further out than the data plate says, don't lift it. Ask your supervisor.

V:4:4:0.t: You need the weight before you can compare it with the rated capacity. Here's a pallet with five layers of eight cartons. Each carton is twenty kilos, and the pallet is twenty-five.

V:4:4:1.t: Count. Five layers times eight cartons is forty cartons.

V:4:4:2.t: Multiply. Forty cartons times twenty kilos is eight hundred kilos.

V:4:4:3.t: Add the pallet. Eight hundred plus twenty-five is eight hundred and twenty-five kilos.

V:4:5:0.t: Where do you find the weight?

V:4:5:1.t: Look for labels and markings on the load.

V:4:5:2.t: Check the consignment note or running sheet.

V:4:5:3.t: Weighbridge dockets show what was weighed.

V:4:5:4.t: Manufacturers' documents list the weight of machines and tanks.

V:4:5:5.t: And if you can't find the weight, don't lift it. Ask your supervisor.

V:4:6:0.t: This forklift has a clamp attachment fitted instead of plain tynes.

V:4:6:1.t: It does a special job, but it also changes how much the forklift can safely lift.

V:4:7:0.t: Attachments change how much you can lift.

V:4:7:1.t: They add weight and push the load further out, so capacity goes down.

V:4:7:2.t: Only use attachments approved by the manufacturer, with a data plate that matches.

V:4:7:3.t: With a jib, the hanging load can swing. Move slowly and smoothly.

V:4:7:4.t: With a rotator, keep the load low and the forklift stopped while you rotate.

V:4:7:5.t: And only ever lift a person in a purpose-built work platform. Never on the tynes or a pallet.

V:4:8:1.t: If a load is heavier on one side, centre it on the tynes, or have it restacked.

V:4:8:2.t: Long or wide loads swing out on turns. Give them extra room and use a spotter.

V:4:8:3.t: Liquids slosh around and push the forklift. Accelerate, brake and turn smoothly and slowly.

V:4:8:4.t: And if there's no pallet, put the load on timber gluts or dunnage, so you can get the tynes in and out.

V:4:9:0.t: That's Module 4. Keep the centre of gravity inside the triangle, and never go over the rated capacity. Next up is the maths — and we'll go through it step by step.

V:5:0:0.t: Module 5 is the maths. Don't worry — we'll go slowly, one step at a time. Pause the video whenever you like and try it yourself.

V:5:1:1.t: Use a calculator. There's one built into the quizzes.

V:5:1:2.t: Write every step down. That's what you'll do in your assessment too.

V:5:1:3.t: And take your time. Check your answer makes sense.

V:5:2:0.t: Rated capacity is in kilograms, but paperwork sometimes uses tonnes.

V:5:2:1.t: One tonne is one thousand kilograms.

V:5:2:2.t: So to change tonnes into kilograms, times by one thousand. One point five tonnes is fifteen hundred kilograms.

V:5:3:0.t: Here's a pallet with five layers. Each layer has ten cartons. Each carton is twenty kilos, and the pallet is thirty.

V:5:3:1.t: Count. Five layers times ten cartons is fifty cartons.

V:5:3:2.t: Multiply. Fifty cartons times twenty kilos is one thousand kilos.

V:5:3:3.t: Add the pallet. One thousand plus thirty is one thousand and thirty kilos.

V:5:4:0.t: A weighbridge weighs the whole truck. To get the load, take the empty truck away from the loaded truck.

V:5:4:1.t: The loaded truck weighs eighteen thousand kilos.

V:5:4:2.t: The empty truck weighs twelve thousand.

V:5:4:3.t: So the load is six thousand kilos.

V:5:4:4.t: If that's four pallets that are all the same, divide by four. Each pallet is fifteen hundred kilos.

V:5:5:0.t: Sometimes you need the most cartons you can carry. Your limit is one thousand kilos, the pallet is twenty, and each carton is thirty.

V:5:5:1.t: First, take the pallet off the limit. One thousand take away twenty is nine hundred and eighty.

V:5:5:2.t: Then divide by the carton weight. Nine hundred and eighty divided by thirty is thirty-two point six seven.

V:5:5:3.t: Always round down. So the answer is thirty-two cartons.

V:5:5:4.t: Why not round up? Thirty-three cartons would be one thousand and ten kilos. That's too heavy.

V:5:6:0.t: Now the load centre. It's the distance from the front of the tynes to the middle of the load's weight.

V:5:6:1.t: For an even load pushed right back against the backrest, it's half the depth of the load.

V:5:6:2.t: This crate is twelve hundred millimetres deep. Half of twelve hundred is six hundred millimetres.

V:5:7:0.t: If there's a gap between the load and the backrest, add the gap.

V:5:7:1.t: This crate is a thousand millimetres deep, so half is five hundred. The gap is two hundred. Five hundred plus two hundred is seven hundred millimetres.

V:5:7:2.t: Seven hundred is further out than the six hundred on the data plate. So push the tynes all the way in, with the load against the backrest.

V:5:8:0.t: Now compare the load with the rated capacity. Forklift A's data plate says twenty-five hundred kilos at a six hundred millimetre load centre.

V:5:8:1.t: Our pallet weighs nineteen hundred kilos, and its load centre is six hundred millimetres.

V:5:8:2.t: Nineteen hundred is less than twenty-five hundred. It's OK to lift, with six hundred kilos to spare.

V:5:9:0.t: This crate's paperwork says two point seven tonnes. Times by one thousand: twenty-seven hundred kilos.

V:5:9:1.t: The rated capacity is twenty-five hundred kilos.

V:5:9:2.t: Twenty-seven hundred is two hundred kilos too heavy. Do not lift it.

V:5:10:0.t: How many six hundred kilo drums can it carry at once? Divide the rated capacity by the weight of one drum. Twenty-five hundred divided by six hundred is four point one seven.

V:5:10:1.t: Always round down. So the answer is four drums.

V:5:10:2.t: Five drums would be three thousand kilos. That's too heavy.

V:5:11:0.t: That's the maths. Work out the weight, check the load centre, then compare it with the rated capacity. Have a go at the quiz — and use the calculator.

V:6:0:0.t: Module 6 is about driving safely, ramps, picking up loads, stacking, and loading trucks.

V:6:1:0.t: When you travel, keep the load low — about a hundred to a hundred and fifty millimetres off the ground — and tilt the mast back.

V:6:1:1.t: Look the way you're going. If the load blocks your view, drive in reverse, or use a spotter.

V:6:1:2.t: Seatbelt on, no passengers ever, and slow down at corners, doorways and intersections.

V:6:2:0.t: On a ramp with a load, keep the load on the uphill side. Drive forwards up, and reverse down.

V:6:3:0.t: With no load, it's the other way around. Keep the tynes pointing downhill. Reverse up, and drive forwards down.

V:6:3:1.t: And never turn on a ramp or drive across it.

V:6:4:0.t: Before you move any load, do a trial lift. Lift it just clear of the ground, and stop.

V:6:4:1.t: Is the forklift steady? Is the load secure and balanced? If the back wheels feel light, lower it straight away.

V:6:5:0.t: When you stack in racking, follow these steps.

V:6:5:2.t: Only raise or lower a load when you're stopped. Never while moving.

V:6:5:3.t: Level the tynes, then inch forward slowly.

V:6:5:4.t: Lower the load onto the beams, back out, and lower the tynes to travel height before you drive off.

V:6:6:1.t: Make sure the truck can't move. Brakes on, wheels chocked, and the driver somewhere safe.

V:6:6:2.t: Set up an exclusion zone around the truck.

V:6:6:3.t: Check the dock plate is secure, and rated for the forklift and the load.

V:6:6:4.t: And keep well back from the dock edge.

V:6:7:0.t: That's Module 6. Keep it low, keep it slow, and look where you're going. Read the lessons and try the quiz.

V:7:0:0.t: Module 7, the last one. How to park and shut down, change a gas bottle, and charge a battery safely.

V:7:1:0.t: At the end of the shift, the job isn't over until the forklift is parked safely.

V:7:1:1.t: This one runs on LPG. You can see the gas cylinder on the back.

V:7:2:0.t: When you finish, park in a safe, level area. Never block exits, walkways, fire equipment or switchboards.

V:7:2:1.t: Select neutral. Put the park brake on. Lower the tynes flat on the ground.

V:7:2:2.t: Turn it off, isolate the power, take the key, and report any defects from your shift.

V:7:3:0.t: Changing an L P G gas bottle? Do it in a well-ventilated area, with no flames and no smoking.

V:7:3:1.t: Wear gloves and eye protection. L P G is so cold it can burn your skin.

V:7:3:2.t: Close the valve, let the engine run until it stops, then swap the bottle. Make sure the locating pin is in and the bottle is secure.

V:7:3:3.t: Check for leaks with soapy water. Bubbles mean a leak. Never use a flame.

V:7:4:0.t: Charging a forklift battery gives off hydrogen gas, which can explode. Only charge in the charging area, with good airflow.

V:7:4:1.t: Turn the charger off before you connect or disconnect the battery, so there's no spark.

V:7:4:2.t: Battery acid burns. Wear your P P E, and know where the eyewash station is.
